questions.q: Which pair among the following does not have the same bond order?

questions.solution:
Electron gain enthalpy increases with decrease in atomic size. On moving from left to right in the periodic table, the atomic size decreases and electron gain enthalpy increase for fluorine.
In case of oxygen, due to its small size and compact nature, the incoming electron is not accomodated with ease resulting into low electron gain enthalpy than sulphur. So the correct order of electron gain enthalpy is $\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{S} \gt \mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{N}$.

questions.q: If the mole fraction of ethanol in a solution of ethanol in water is 0.050 , then find the molarity of the given solution.

Mass of ethanol $=0.05 \times 46=2.3 \mathrm{~g}$.
Mass of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}=0.95 \times 18=17.1 \mathrm{~g}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Pressure of $1 \mathrm{~g}$ ideal gas $X$ at $300 \mathrm{~K}$ is $2 \mathrm{~atm}$. When $2 \mathrm{~g}$ of another gas $Y$ is introduced in the same vessel at same temperature, the pressure become $\mathrm{l}$ atm. The correct relationship between molar masses of $X$ and $Y$ is

Given,
Initially,
$\begin{array}{ll}p=2 \mathrm{~atm}, & T=300 \mathrm{~K} \\ V=v \mathrm{~L}, & m_x=1 \mathrm{~g}\end{array}
Finally,
$\begin{array}{rlrl}p & =2+1 & T & =300 \mathrm{~K} \\ & =3 \mathrm{~atm} & m_y & =2 \mathrm{~g}\end{array}
$\quad V=v \mathrm{~L}$
Let molar mass of gas $X$ and $Y$ be $M_x$ and $M_y$ respectively. Applying ideal gas equation to initial and final conditions.
Initially, $2 \times V=\frac{1}{M_x} R T$ ...(i)
Finally, $3 \times V=\left(\frac{1}{M_x}+\frac{2}{M_y}\right) R T$....(ii)
Dividing (i) by (ii), we get
$M_y=4 M_x$.

Precision $= \pm 1 \%\therefore$ Accuracy $=0.01\begin{aligned} & \Delta v=3 \times 10^8 \times \frac{2}{100}=6 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \Delta x=1.05 \times 10^{-13} \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The volume of a spherical ball is increasing at a rate of $4 \pi \mathrm{cm}^3 \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. The rate at which its radius increases, when its volume is $288 \pi \mathrm{cm}^3$, is.......$\mathrm{cm} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$

To find, $r / d t=$ ?

On differentiating w.r.t. $t$,

From Eq. (ii), we get
$\frac{d r}{d t}=\frac{1}{r^2}=\frac{1}{6^2}=\frac{1}{36}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Find the coordinates of a point on the curve $y=x^2-3 x+2$, at which the tangent drawn to this curve is perpendicular to the line $y=x$.
questions.solution:
Given curve, $y=x^2-3 x+2$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$,
$\frac{d y}{d x}=2 x-3$
Which represents the slope of tangent drawn to the curve.
$m_1=2 x-3$  ...(i)
Given line, $\quad y=x$ ...(ii)
On comparing with $y=m x+c$
Slope of line (ii), $m_2=1\therefore$ Tangent to the curve is perpendicular to line (ii).
$\therefore \quad m_1 \cdot m_2=-1m_1 \cdot 1=-1\begin{array}{cc}\Rightarrow & m_1=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 x-3=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 x=2 \\ \Rightarrow & x=1\end{array}
$\therefore \quad y=(1)^2-3 \times 1+2y=0\therefore$ Point of tangent drawn $=(1,0)

questions.q: The probability for a contractor to get a road contract is $\frac{2}{9}$ and to get a building contract is $\frac{5}{9}$, if the probability to get both the contract is $\frac{1}{6}$, then what is the probability to get neither of these two contracts?
questions.solution:
Let $A$ be the event of getting a road contract and $B$ be the event of getting a building contract.
$\therefore \quad P(A)=\frac{2}{9}, P(B)=\frac{5}{9}P(A \cap B)=\frac{1}{6}\therefore \quad P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)\begin{aligned} & =\frac{2}{9}+\frac{5}{9}-\frac{1}{6} \\ & =\frac{7}{9}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{14-3}{18}=\frac{11}{18}\end{aligned}\therefore \quad P\left((A \cup B)^{\prime}\right)=1-P(A \cup B)=1-\frac{11}{18}=\frac{7}{18}$
Hence, the probability to get neither of these two contracts is $7 / 18$.

$\begin{aligned} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left[\frac{-16 \tan ^2 x}{x^2\left(1-\tan ^2 x\right)\left(1-3 \tan ^2 x\right)}\right] \\ & =-16 \lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{\tan x}{x}\right)^2 \lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\left(1-\tan ^2 x\right)\left(1-3 \tan ^2 x\right)} \\ & =-16(1)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{1 \cdot 1}=-16\end{aligned}$

$|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}|=1$

questions.solution:

$\Delta E=12.1 \mathrm{eV}$
i.e. final energy of excited state,
$E_2=\frac{-13.6 \mathrm{eV}}{n^2}$
We know that, $E_2-E_1=\Delta E\Rightarrow \quad E_2=\Delta E+E_1$
Substituting the value, we get
$\begin{aligned} & -\frac{13.6}{n^2}=[12.1+(-13.6)] \\ & -\frac{13.6}{n^2}=-1.50 \Rightarrow x^2=9.07 \Rightarrow n \simeq 3\end{aligned}$

Then, number of spectral lines emitted by $\mathrm{H}$-atom
$=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=\frac{3(3-1)}{2}=3$

questions.q:
Assertion (A) Two condensers of same capacity are connected first in parallel and then in series. The ratio of resultant capacities in the two cases will be $4: 1$.
Reason ( $R$ ) In parallel, capacity increases and in series capacity decreases.
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is a correct explanation for $\mathrm{A}$.
Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not a correct explanation for A.
questions.solution:
Given, two capacitors of same capacities $C$.
In series, equivalent capacitance is given by
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{C_S}=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}=\frac{1}{C}+\frac{1}{C}=\frac{2}{C} \\ & C_S=\frac{C}{2}\end{aligned}$
In parallel, equivalent capacitance is given by
$C_P=C_1+C_2=C+C=2 C$
Ratio $=\frac{C_P}{C_S}=\frac{2 C}{\left(\frac{C}{2}\right)}=\frac{4}{1}\Rightarrow \quad C_P: C_S=4: 1$
Hence, Assertion is true
In parallel, $C_P \gt C$
In series, $C_S \lt  C$
So, in parallel, capacity is increased but in series, capacity is decreased.
Hence, Reason is also true, but it is not the correct explanation of Assertion.

Assertion (A) The colour of radiation does not change on passing through different media.
Reason (R) The media do not absorb or emit colours.
options: Both $A$ and $R$ are true and $R$ is a correct explanation for $A$.
Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true but $\mathrm{R}$ is not a correct explanation for $\mathrm{A}$.
A is false but $R$ is true.
questions.solution:
The colour of radiation does not change on passing through different media. This is because, when light radiation passes through different media, only wavelength and speed changes, but frequency remains same and colour of light radiation depends only on frequency.
Hence, Assertion (A) is true.
"The media do not absorb or emit colours" this statement is wrong. Because the absorption or emission of colours of radiation depends only on the nature of medium.
Hence, Reason is false.

questions.solution:
Given, radius of Earth and Mars are $6400 \mathrm{~km}$ and $3200 \mathrm{~km}$, respectively.
Mass of Earth $=10$ (Mass of Mars)
$M_e=10 M_m$
We know that, acceleration due to gravity at surface of a planet is
$g=\frac{G M}{R^2},$
where, $M=$ mass of planet
and $R=$ radius of planet.
Taking the ratio of acceleration due to gravity of Mars to Earth,
$\frac{g_m}{g_e}=\frac{\frac{G M_m}{R_m^2}}{\frac{G M_e}{R_e^2}}=\frac{M_m}{M_e} \times\left(\frac{R_e}{R_m}\right)^2$
By substituting the values, we get
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{g_m}{g_e}=\frac{1}{10} \times\left(\frac{6400}{3200}\right)^2=\frac{1}{10} \times 4 \\ & g_m=\frac{2}{5} g_e\end{aligned}$
Given, the weight on earth's surface,
$w_e=m g_e=200 \mathrm{~N}\therefore$ Weight on the Mars surface,
$w_m=m g_m=\frac{2}{5}\left(m g_e\right)=\frac{2}{5} \times 200 \mathrm{~N}=80 \mathrm{~N}$

$C=\frac{4 \times 10^{-2} \times 5 \times 10^{-2} \times 5 \times 10^{-3}}{0.2}=5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{Nm} \mathrm{rad}^{-1}$
Current sensitivity,

questions.q: A square frame of side $1 \mathrm{~m}$ carrying a current $I$ produces a magnetic field $B$ at its centre. The same current is passed through a circular coil having the same perimeter as the square. The magnetic field at the centre of the circular coil is $B^{\prime}$. The ratio of $\frac{B}{B^{\prime}}$ is

Using, $B=4\left[\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi r}\left(\sin 45^{\circ}+\sin 45^{\circ}\right)\right]\Rightarrow \quad B=\frac{4 \mu_0 I}{4 \pi\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \Rightarrow B=\frac{2 \mu_0 I}{\pi a} \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}B=\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_0 I}{\pi a}$ ...(i) For circle, Let $R$ be the radius of circular coil. Then, $2 \pi R=4 a\Rightarrow \quad R=\frac{4 a}{2 \pi}=\frac{2 a}{\pi}$ Using the expression for magnetic field at centre of circular coil, $B^{\prime}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}\Rightarrow \quad B^{\prime}=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\left(\frac{2 a}{\pi}\right)}=\frac{\mu_0 \pi I}{4 a}$ ...(ii) From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $\frac{B}{B^{\prime}}=\frac{\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_0 I}{\pi a}}{\frac{\mu_0 \pi I}{4 a}}=\frac{8 \sqrt{2}}{\pi^2}$

Final surface area, $A_2=4 \pi R^2$

$=\frac{(10 r)^2}{1000 r^2}=\frac{100 r^2}{1000 r^2}=\frac{1}{10}$ or $1: 10$

Assertion (A) At critical temperature, surface tension of liquids become zero.
Reason (R) At critical temperature, intermolecular forces for liquids and gases become equal.
options: Both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true and $\mathrm{R}$ is a correct explanation for $A$.
Both $A$ and $R$ are true but $R$ is not a correct explanation for $\mathrm{A}$.
questions.solution:
Critical temperature is temperature at which surface tension of liquid become zero. So it is true. At critical temperature, the intermolecular force between liquid molecules become very weak due to which interaction between molecules vanishes.
Hence, surface tension reduces. So, Reason (R) is also true and is a correct explanation for Assertion (A).

Velocity of object opposite to train, $v_0=5 \mathrm{~km} \mathrm{~h}^{-1}\begin{aligned} & =\frac{25}{18} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \\ & =1.39 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\end{aligned}$

Relative velocity of train w.r.t object $v_{\text {rel }}=v_t+v_0$

questions.q: A bob of a pendulum of length $0.5 \mathrm{~m}$ has a speed of $6 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ at its lowest point. Find the speed of the bob when the string of the pendulum makes $60^{\circ}$ with the vertical, (take $\left.g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Given, length of pendulum, $l=0.5 \mathrm{~m}$
Speed at lowest point, $v_1=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Angle made by string with vertical, $\theta=60^{\circ}$ In $\triangle O B C, \frac{O C}{O B}=\cos \theta=\cos 60^{\circ}\frac{l-h}{l}=\cos 60^{\circ}\Rightarrow \quad h=l\left(1-\cos 60^{\circ}\right)h=0.5\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right)=0.25 \mathrm{~m}$ Using law of conservation of mechanical energy, we get $\begin{aligned} & K_i+U_i=K_f+U_f \\ & \frac{1}{2} m v_1^2+0=\frac{1}{2} m v_2^2+m g h\end{aligned}$ [Taking initial potential energy at ground is equal to zero.] $\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} m v_2^2 & =\frac{1}{2} m v_1^2-m g h \\ v_2^2 & =v_1^2-2 g h\end{aligned}$ Substituting the values, we get $v_2=\sqrt{(6)^2-2 \times 10 \times 0.25}=\sqrt{31} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Hence, the final velocity at an angle $60^{\circ}$ is $\sqrt{31} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

questions.q: A disc of mass $4 \mathrm{~kg}$ and radius $0.4 \mathrm{~m}$ is rotating with angular velocity $30 \mathrm{rad} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$. When two point-masses, each $0.25 \mathrm{~kg}$ are attached on the periphery of the disc, at diametrically opposite points, its angular velocity becomes
questions.solution:
Given, mass of disc, $M=4 \mathrm{~kg}$
Radius of disc, $R=0.4 \mathrm{~m}$
Initial angular velocity of disc, $\omega_1=30 \mathrm{rad} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$
Mass of point-masses, $m=0.25 \mathrm{~kg}$
Now, moment of inertia of disc, $I_1=\frac{1}{2} M R^2$
Moment of inertia of disc and two point mass system,
$I_2=\frac{1}{2} M R^2+2 m R^2$
Let $\omega_2$ be the final angular velocity.
According to conservation of angular momentum,
$I_1 \omega_1=I_2 \omega_2 \Rightarrow \omega_2=I_1 \omega_1 / I_2$
Substituting the values, we get
$\omega_2=\frac{\frac{1}{2} M R^2(30)}{\left(\frac{1}{2} M R^2+2 m R^2\right)}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times(0.4)^2 \times 30}{\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times(0.4)^2+2 \times 0.25 \times(0.4)^2}\omega_2=24 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$
Hence, the final angular velocity of system is $24 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$.

questions.solution:

Using, the acceleration produced in body rolling down the inclined plane $a=\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+\frac{I_{\mathrm{CM}}}{M R^2}}=\frac{g \sin \theta}{1+\beta}$ ...(i) By using equation of motion, $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2$ where $u=0$ (initial velocity) $t=$ time taken to reach at bottom. $s=0+\frac{1}{2} \frac{g \sin \theta}{(1+\beta)} t^2\Rightarrow \quad t^2=\frac{2 s(1+\beta)}{g \sin \theta}$ But, from the diagram, $\frac{h}{s}=\sin \theta\Rightarrow \quad s=\frac{h}{\sin \theta}$ Substituting the value of $s$, we get $\begin{aligned} t & =\sqrt{\frac{2 h(1+\beta)}{g \sin ^2 \theta}} \\ & =\frac{1}{\sin \theta} \sqrt{\frac{2 h(1+\beta)}{g}}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the ratio of amplitudes of two interfering waves is $4: 3$, then the ratio of maximum and minimum intensity is
questions.solution:
Given, the ratio of amplitudes of two 
interfering waves is $4: 3$
i.e $\frac{A_1}{A_2}=\frac{4}{3}$  ...(i)
We know that, intensity of wave is proportional to square of amplitude.
$\therefore \frac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\frac{A_{\max }}{A_{\min }}\right)^2$, where maximum and minimum amplitudes are
$A_{\text {max }}=A_1+A_2$
and $\quad A_{\min }=A_1-A_2$
Substituting the values, we get
$\frac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\frac{A_1+A_2}{A_1-A_2}\right)^2$
Multiplying and dividing by $A_2^2$ in RHS, we get.
$\frac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\frac{\frac{A_1}{A_2}+1}{\frac{A_1}{A_2}-1}\right)^2=\left(\frac{\frac{4}{3}+1}{\frac{4}{3}-1}\right)^2=\left(\frac{7}{1}\right)^2=\frac{49}{1}$

questions.q: A body of mass $M$ is dropped from a height $h$ on a sand floor. If the body penetrates $x \mathrm{~cm}$ into the sand, then the average resistance offered by the sand to the body is
questions.solution:
Given, mass of body $=M$
Height above the sand floor $=h$
Distance penetrated into sand $=x$
Let $v$ be the velocity with which body strikes the surface.
Then, by equation of motion, we get
$v^2=u^2+2 g h \Rightarrow v^2=2 g h$  ...(i)
$[\because$ Initial velocity at highest point, $u=0]$
With this velocity $v$, when body passes through the sand floor it comes to rest after travelling a distance $x$.
Let $F$ be the resisting force acting on body.
Then, net downward force will be
$F_{\text {net }}=M g-F$
By work-energy theorem, work done by all forces is equal to change in $\mathrm{KE}$, which gives
$\therefore \quad W=\Delta KF_{\text {net }} \times x=K_f-K_i(M g-F) x=0-\frac{1}{2} M v^2 \quad\left[\because\right.$ Final KE, $\left.K_f=0\right]\Rightarrow \quad(M g-F) x=-\frac{1}{2} M v^2$ ...(ii)
Substituting the value from Eq. (i) in Eq. (ii), we get
$\Rightarrow \quad M g x-F x=-\frac{1}{2} M(2 g h)M g x-F x=-M g h\Rightarrow \quad F x=M g x+M g h \Rightarrow F=M g\left(\frac{x+h}{x}\right)$
